# WebApp Subsystem API & Service Specification

The WebApp subsystem provides a developer introspection, source code exploration, and static analysis platform
for the **KernelInfo-Parser** repository. It features a modular FastAPI REST backend and a zero-build vanilla
ES-Module IDE frontend.

## 1. Architectural Overview & Component Structure

The WebApp is structured into a zero-trust, decoupled layered architecture:

```
webapp/
├── backend/
│   ├── app.py                      # FastAPI application factory & middleware setup
│   ├── config.py                   # Centralized configuration resolver (via core.config)
│   ├── models.py                   # Pydantic request schema of the patch formatter
│   ├── data/email_domains.json     # Email domain -> organization for release statistics (§4.10)
│   ├── database/
│   │   ├── pool.py                 # `get_reader()` entry point over the configured engine's read sessions
│   │   └── helpers.py              # Encoding safeguards, version metadata lookup
│   ├── security/
│   │   ├── jail.py                 # Canonical filesystem sandboxing & jail validation

│   │   ├── sql.py                  # SQL LIKE wildcard sanitizer & identifier validation
│   │   └── middleware.py           # Security headers (CSP), sliding-window rate limiter, repository selection (pure ASGI)

│   │   ├── git_reader.py           # Persistent Git object readers (git cat-file --batch), up to 4 per repository
│   │   ├── docs_service.py         # Documentation label index & kernel-doc comment extraction
```

## 2. Security & Zero-Trust Sandbox Specifications

### 2.1. Repository Path Jailing (`webapp/backend/security/jail.py`)
All file requests are validated against `LINUX_REPO_DIR` (the root of the tracked kernel git tree).
- `resolve_and_verify_repo_path(relative_path: str) -> Path`: Resolves the canonical path (`resolve()`) and
  verifies that `resolved_path.is_relative_to(LINUX_REPO_DIR)`.
- Path traversal sequences (`..`, `../`, `//`, null bytes) trigger immediate `HTTP 400 Bad Request`.
- Accessing files outside the repository jail triggers `HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN`.
- **Patch paths** (P1, `patch_apply.safe_path`): every path named by a mailing-list patch header must be
  relative, without `..`, empty segments, backslashes, NUL or a leading `.git/`; a violation fails that file
  (*path outside the tree*), not the request. Patched files are read from Git and held in memory only.

### 2.1.1. Git Revision & Object-Spec Validation (`webapp/backend/security/git.py`)
Every endpoint names a revision (a version name, a branch or a commit SHA) and the services pass it
to `git` as a **positional argument** (`git blame <rev> -- <path>`). Git reads an argument starting
with `-` as an option, so an unvalidated revision becomes one: `--contents=<file>` makes `git blame`
print any file, and `--output=<file>` makes `git log` write one. A revision is therefore validated
before it can reach a command line:
- `safe_rev(rev) -> str`: returns the revision, or raises `HTTP 400 Bad Request`. Accepts only
  `core.globalstuff.is_safe_git_rev()`: a name of at most 255 characters starting with `[A-Za-z0-9]`
  and otherwise limited to `[A-Za-z0-9._/+-]`, which covers tags (`v2.6.32-rc1`), branches
  (`origin/master`, `feature/x`) and full or short SHAs, and excludes options, whitespace, newlines
  and every character git gives a meaning in a revision expression (`^`, `~`, `:`, `{`, `}`).
- `is_safe_rev(rev) -> bool`: the non-raising form, for services that fall back instead of failing
  (`TreeResolverService.resolve_commit_sha()` returns `None`, so callers answer 404 as before).
- `<rev>:<path>` specs for `git cat-file --batch` are checked with `core.globalstuff.is_safe_git_spec()`.
  The stream reads one request per line: a newline or NUL inside a spec injects further requests and
  desynchronizes every later answer on that long-lived stream, so such specs are never written to it:
  `GitReader` (`git_reader.py`) answers `missing`, and `history_service.batch_blob_shas()` — which
  matches answers to specs by position — leaves the offending spec out and reports `None` for it.

Validation points (every revision a service passes to git goes through one of them):
`GitService.get_blame()` / `get_file_history()` (`safe_rev`), `_cached_git_file_history()`
(`is_safe_rev`), `KconfigService._rev()` (the single funnel for that service's `git grep` /
`ls-tree` calls), `GitTreeResolver.resolve_commit_sha()` (Path C, and therefore the filesystem,
diff, docs and history services), `HistoryService.get_change_commits()`, and
`database/helpers.get_version_info()`, whose `git rev-parse` fallback is skipped for a name that
would be read as an option (the unresolved name is still returned, so callers answer 404).
`GitService.get_commit_diff()` keeps its stricter 4–40 hex check (`_HEX_REF`).

### 2.1.2. Identifier Validation for Git Pattern Searches (`webapp/backend/security/sql.py`)
A caller-supplied name also reaches `git grep` as a **pattern**, where metacharacters match far more
than the name itself: `CONFIG_.*` finds every `CONFIG_` reference in the tree (44,485 lines at v3.0,
3.0 MiB, versus 406 for a real symbol), and the whole result would be read, parsed and cached under
a name the caller chose. `KconfigService._safe_symbol()` therefore strips the `CONFIG_` prefix and
rejects anything `is_valid_identifier()` does not accept (`^[A-Za-z0-9_.~+-]+$`) with
`HTTP 400 Bad Request`; it is the gate for `get_symbol_usage()` and `kbuild_usage()`. Patterns built
from an accepted name are still escaped (`re.escape`, as `_other_arch_definitions()` does), the
literal searches pass `-F` so git reads the name as text rather than a basic regex, and a symbol
with more than `_USAGE_REF_LIMIT` (20,000) references is reported `source_refs_truncated: true`
(the KConfig view shows its count as `20000+`) instead of being cached whole. `git grep -E` itself uses a DFA,
so a pattern cannot make it
backtrack; the control here is over how much it can match and retain.

### 2.1.3. Text Search over a Revision (`webapp/backend/services/grep_service.py`, `webapp/backend/security/git.py`)
Every feature that searches source text (full-text code search, §5.34; tracepoint call sites, §4.9) goes
through `grep_service.grep()`, so the same validation, limits and caching apply everywhere:
- **Revision**: resolved to its commit SHA first (`git_tree_resolver.resolve_commit_sha()`, which applies
  `is_safe_rev`); git greps the SHA, never the caller's name. An unknown revision answers `404`.
- **Pattern** (`validate_grep_pattern`): 1–256 characters, no NUL, CR or LF, always passed after `-e` (a
  leading `-` is text). `mode=fixed` uses `-F`; `mode=regex` uses POSIX ERE (`-E`). PCRE (`-P`) is never
  offered. A pattern git rejects (`a(`) answers `400`.
- **Path filters** (`validate_pathspecs`, `git_pathspecs`): at most 8, each at most 200 characters, relative,
  no `..` segment, no leading `/` or `:` (callers never supply pathspec magic). The server adds it:
  `:(glob)<spec>` for an include, `:(exclude,glob)<spec>` for `!<spec>`; a wildcard without `/` matches in
  every directory (`*.c` → `**/*.c`); a plain path matches the file or the directory below it. An exclusion
  alone excludes from the whole tree. Violations answer `400`.
- **Command**: `git -c color.grep.<slot>=normal… grep -n -I -z --color=always <-F|-E> [-i] [-w]
  [--max-count=N] -e <pattern> <sha> -- <pathspecs>`. Every colour slot except `matchSelected` prints nothing,
  so the only escape sequences mark matches, and the match ranges (`[[start, end], …]`, character offsets in
  the decoded line) follow git's own regex semantics. `--max-count` exists since Git 2.38 (detected once from
  `git --version`); older gits count per file in Python.
- **Caps**: output is streamed; the process is killed once `max_matches` (default 2,000; the endpoint allows
  at most 20,000, in-process catalogs up to 300,000) or `max_bytes` (8 MiB) is reached (`truncated: true`) or
  after `timeout` (20 s: the partial result is returned with `timed_out: true`). Lines over 500 characters are
  clipped around their first match (`clipped: true`, ranges shifted).
- **Concurrency**: a semaphore per repository allows 2 greps at a time; a third caller waits up to 5 s, then
  gets `503 {"detail": "search busy, retry"}`. The rate limiter (§2.4) still applies.
- **Cache**: `RepoScopedCache(maxsize=128)` keyed by `(sha, pattern, mode, flags, paths, caps)`. A commit's
  content never changes, so entries are never invalidated by sync tokens; a timed-out result is never cached.
- **Result**: `{sha, matches: [{path, line, text, ranges, clipped}], files, total, truncated, timed_out,
  elapsed_ms}`.

### 2.2. SQL Wildcard Handling
Services pass raw text to the spec `like(text, mode, ci=)` helper, which escapes `%`, `_` and the
escape character and emits the `ESCAPE` clause of the active dialect, so wildcard queries like `q=%` neither
match everything nor turn an anchored prefix into a full scan. Search texts are truncated to 100 characters by the
service. `webapp/backend/security/sql.py` holds:
- `is_valid_identifier(name: str) -> bool`: `^[A-Za-z0-9_.~+-]+$`, the gate described in §2.1.2.

### 2.3. HTTP Security Headers (`webapp/backend/security/middleware.py`)
Every response includes hardened security headers:
- `Content-Security-Policy`: `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src
  'self' data: blob:; connect-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. Scripts and workers are restricted to
  `'self'`, with `'unsafe-inline'` only for style attributes. `script-src` carries **no** `'unsafe-eval'`: no
  frontend module evaluates code from a string (no `eval`, no `new Function`), so allowing it would only widen
  what an injected string could do. A route may set a stricter policy of its own (`GET /api/fs/raw/...`
  sandboxes raw SVG); the middleware only fills in the default.
- `X-Frame-Options`: `DENY` (prevents clickjacking attacks).
- `X-Content-Type-Options`: `nosniff`.
- `Referrer-Policy`: `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`.

### 2.3.1. CORS (`webapp/backend/app.py`)
The API carries no cookie or header authentication, so any origin may read it (`allow_origins=["*"]`,
methods `GET`, `POST`, `OPTIONS`) but **never with credentials** (`allow_credentials=False`). The two
combined are what Starlette turns into a reflected `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` plus
`Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, which would let any page in a visitor's browser read this
API as that visitor; with credentials off, the literal `*` is returned instead. Because the frontend
is served from the same origin, it still reads `X-KIP-Sync` and every other response header.

### 2.4. Sliding-Window Rate Limiting
- `SlidingWindowRateLimiter`: Enforces an in-memory sliding window cap (default 600 requests / 60 seconds per
  client IP) on `/api/` requests; the shell, `/boot.js` and the build's assets are not limited, whatever their
  extension, while an API path ending in `.js` or `.json` is. Exceeding requests receive `HTTP 429 Too Many
  Requests` with a `Retry-After` header. Behind a reverse proxy every client shares the proxy's address.
- The security headers, the rate limiter, `RepoContextMiddleware` and `SyncHeaderMiddleware` are pure ASGI
  middleware (`BaseHTTPMiddleware` would run each request through an extra task and memory stream).

### 2.5. Strict Read-Only Database & Parser-First Feature Invariant
The `webapp/` backend operates exclusively as a read-only presentation and query tier. Under no circumstances
may any router, service, middleware, or background task in `webapp/` execute database schema definitions (DDL:
`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`) or data modification commands (DML: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`,
`REPLACE`).
- **Propose Parser Changes for DB Writes & New Features**: Whenever a new or modified `webapp/` feature would
  require database writes, new tables or columns, or non-trivial source/commit parsing, the change must be
  proposed and implemented in the parser engine (`core/DBLayout.py`, `main.py`, `parser/`, `core/backfills.py`),
  never via database writes or primary parsing logic inside `webapp/`.
- **Parser-First Execution with Unparsed `"git"` Fallback**: Instead of implementing webapp-side parsing to
  deliver a feature, push extraction and persistence to the parser (and provide a resumable CLI backfill in
  `core/backfills.py` when adding tables for already-ingested versions). In `webapp/`, always query the
  parser-populated database tables first for parsed versions (`vid != 0`), retaining an on-demand `"git"`
  fallback path (reusing pure `parser/` extraction modules where applicable) strictly for revisions not yet
  parsed in the database (see §2.16 `m_commit_relation`, §2.17 `m_commit_release`, §2.19 `m_blob_facts`, and
  `m_kbuild_symbol`).
- All table creations, schema migrations, and initial seed rows (including `m_db_instance`) are the strict and
  exclusive responsibility of the parser engine (`core/DBLayout.py`, `main.py`).
- All web application database queries route through the declarative read session of the configured engine: `with get_reader() as reader:` (`webapp/backend/database/pool.py`; `Engine.reader()` of `database.engine`, a `ReadSession`, `SQLiteReadSession` or `MockReadSession` adhering to `ReadAPI`). The engine is chosen by `_reader_engine()` in that module (the one selection seam); tests serve `get_reader()` from a `MockDB` / `SQLiteDB(":memory:")` with `patch_reader(db)` of `tests/db_fixtures.py`, which patches that seam with `mock.patch`, so production code holds no test hook. Direct raw driver imports (`mysql.connector`) or direct cursor queries outside `db_engine/` are strictly prohibited.
- `ReadSession` exposes typed declarative spec read primitives (`select_rows`, `iter_rows`, `select_one`, `select_values`, `select_value`, `count_rows`, `row_exists`, `aggregate`) with `as_dict=True` default and domain-specific intent methods (`list_network_commits`, `maintainer_sections`, `symbol_name_page`, `symbol_refs_of_targets`, `checkpoint_find_file`, etc.). Write and DDL entry points of a read session raise `ReadOnlyViolation`. There is no raw cursor or SQL text API in `webapp/`.
- Database query interfaces in `webapp/` are strictly read-only and do not support or execute transaction commits.
- Connection Pool (MariaDB engine, private to `db_engine/pool.py`): When `ssh_tunnel` is inactive and a local MariaDB instance is configured, the pool
  connects via Unix domain socket (`/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock`), automatically falling back to TCP
  (`127.0.0.1:3306`) if the socket is inaccessible. When `ssh_tunnel` is enabled in configuration
  (`database.ssh_tunnel.enabled: true`), the pool and FastAPI application startup
  (`webapp/backend/app.py:lifespan`) automatically initialize and verify the SSH tunnel forward
  (`core/ssh_tunnel.py`), reroute pool connection parameters to the forwarded port (`127.0.0.1:<local_port>`),
  and gracefully tear down the tunnel and connection pool on server shutdown.
- Resilient Connection Management: the pool creates itself (and the SSH tunnel before it) once, under
  a lock, whatever the threads asking, and checks it with one connection. The pool (`ConnectionPool`, up to
  `POOL_SIZE` = 32 connections, opened on demand) replaces mysql-connector's `MySQLConnectionPool`, which
  pinged every connection it lent (under a process-wide lock) and reset its session when given back, on top of
  the ping `cursor()` itself makes: three round trips per cursor (3–6 ms over the SSH tunnel, now ~0.7 ms).
  The webapp never changes session state (read only, autocommit, no session variables, temporary tables or
  locks), so a connection goes back as it is. Leasing a connection waits up to `POOL_WAIT_S` (10 s) for a
  connection of a saturated pool, since connections come back as other requests finish (the threadpool has 40
  workers). A read session reconnects a connection that it finds dropped while idle (server
  restart, tunnel drop), and closes instead of reusing one that failed during the request or kept a result it
  could not drain. If connecting fails, the pool resets (at most 3 times) and automatically re-verifies the
  SSH tunnel.
- If expected metadata tables or rows are absent, webapp endpoints must return appropriate HTTP error statuses
  or graceful process-level fallbacks without modifying the underlying database.

### 2.6. Frontend & Service Architectural Invariants
1. **Directory Path Filtering & Polymorphic Navigation**: In database queries on `m_file_blob`, directory
   records have `ftype == 0` while regular files have `ftype != 0`. All file search, path lookup, and
   `#include` header resolution queries explicitly filter `ftype != 0` so directories sharing names or paths
   with header files are never returned as file matches. File viewer endpoints (`get_file`) and frontend code
   views (`virtual_editor.js`) support polymorphic path navigation: opening directory paths returns child
   hierarchies (`entries`, `tree`) and renders interactive navigation tables/grids rather than returning 404
   errors.
2. **Lexical Comment Prioritization & Directive Matching**: In dual-layer syntax and AST overlays
   (`webapp/frontend/js/views/code_view/ast_overlay.js`), lexical tokenizers prioritize matching block
   comments (`/* ... */`) and line comments (`// ...`) *before* general identifier regexes, rendering them as
   non-clickable `<span class="tok-comment">` elements to prevent comment tokens from leaking into
   `.ast-token` or triggering symbol context menus. Preprocessor directive matching on snippet-relative
   coordinate slices allows optional leading hashes (e.g. `^(\s*#?\s*define\s+)`) so directive keywords are
   styled as preprocessors (`tok-macro`) and never tagged as clickable symbol identifiers.
3. **Flat Coordinate Projection & Defensive Navigation**: Symbol detail backend endpoints
   (`webapp/backend/services/symbol_service.py:get_symbol_detail`) expose definition coordinate fields as flat
   scalars (`line: row["line_s"]`, `line_s: row["line_s"]`) at the root of the response payload alongside the
   nested `definition` record. Frontend jump-to-definition callers
   (`webapp/frontend/js/views/code_view/context_menu.js`) resolve coordinates defensively across
   `detail.definition?.line_s || detail.line_s || detail.line || 1` to ensure virtual editors navigate to and
   highlight the exact symbol definition line.
4. **Maintainer Query Sanitization & Parameter Preference**: Developer identity and maintainer endpoints
   (`webapp/backend/routers/maintainers.py`, `webapp/backend/services/maintainer_service.py`) support query
   parameter lookups (`/api/maintainers/{version}/person?email=...`) alongside URL path parameters. Frontend
   API clients sanitize patch trailers and email strings (stripping `<>`, quotes, and whitespace) and prefer
   query parameters when identifiers contain special characters (`@`, `<`, `>`, `/`) to prevent URL decoding
   and route matching failures.
5. **Context Menu Interaction Preservation**: Right-click context menus (`contextmenu`) across webapp
   workspaces (virtual code editor, file explorer sidebar, nodemap canvas) intercept default browser menus and
   offer context-adaptive actions (definitions, references, git blame popovers, command palette search,
   coordinate copying), while strictly preserving primary left-click interactions (inline AST token inspector
   popups, file navigation, node selection) without collision, event race conditions, or lingering ghost
   menus.
6. **Structured Cross-Reference Classification**: Symbol cross-reference backend services (`get_symbol_xref`)
   and frontend inspectors (`showXrefModal`) return and render both primary and multi-declaration definition
   locations (`definitions: [...]` with file path, line bounds, and AST declaration type) alongside usage
   references (`references: [...]` with caller function, file, line, and typed badges `Decl`, `TypeUsage`,
   `Call`, `MemberRef`, `DeclRef`, `MacroExp`; one list, grouped by role), providing direct 1-click jump
   navigation for both definitions and usages. Every location is a location of the requested revision:
   definitions come only from blobs of its Git tree, and the ASTs whose references are looked up are only
   those the symbol's own name identifies, never the shared AST of a marker macro such as `EXPORT_SYMBOL` (see
   §4.3).
7. **Escaping of Interpolated HTML**: every value interpolated into an `innerHTML` / `insertAdjacentHTML`
   template passes through `escapeHtml()` (exported by `webapp/frontend/js/components/modal.js`), including
   error text (`e.message`), repository data (git author names, file paths) and state values (the KConfig
   `arch`). Only values that are *already* rendered HTML are interpolated raw, and those are built from
   escaped parts (`doc_page.js` navigation links, the `virtual_editor.js` build-condition `why` / `ruleHtml`
   fragments). The CSP (§2.3) forbids inline scripts, so this is the layer that keeps repository content from
   entering the DOM as markup.

---

## 2B. Backend Domain & Infrastructure Services

### 2.7. Tri-Path Tree Resolution & Arch-Aware Definition Ranking (`webapp/backend/services/tree_resolver.py`)
1. **Database Tree Resolution (`TreeResolverService`, module singleton `tree_resolver`)**:
   - **Path B (Full-Tree Resolution, `<15ms`, LRU Cached)**: Assembles the entire active `{fnid: blob_id}`
     repository tree at any `commit_id` by loading baseline snapshot records from the `m_checkpoint_tree` view
     (a version's full tree, whether its `m_bridge_checkpoint` rows are full or a delta, `core/API.md` §4.2)
     and chronologically applying forward `m_commit_file` deltas along the first-parent DAG. Results are
     cached in an in-memory `OrderedDict` LRU cache.
   - **Limitation**: Path B only reaches a checkpoint when every first-parent ancestor is ingested in
     `m_commit`/`m_commit_parent`. The parser ingests a bounded commit window, so many intermediate commits
     have broken chains; Path B is therefore used only as a fallback when the Git repository is unavailable.
2. **Git-Native Tree Resolution (`GitTreeResolver`, module singleton `git_tree_resolver`)**:
   - **Path C (Full-Tree Listing, `~50ms` cold, LRU Cached per commit SHA)**: `list_tree(rev)` resolves any
     revision (tag, branch, full/short SHA, even commits never ingested into `m_commit`) via `git rev-parse
     --verify <rev>^{commit}` and returns `{path: blob_sha}` from `git ls-tree -r -z --full-tree`. Submodule
     entries are skipped. This is the authoritative file list for every revision.
   - `list_dir(rev, directory)` returns `(subdirectory names, {path: blob_sha} of the direct files)` from a
     per-commit directory index built in one pass over `list_tree` (`DERIVED_CACHE_SIZE` = 4 commits), so
     expanding a directory avoids scanning the whole tree. `search_index(rev)` is the per-commit list of
     `(lowercased path, lowercased basename, path)` that the file palette scans (`GET /api/fs/search`).
   - `resolve_commit_sha(rev)` answers are cached (4096 entries per repository): a full SHA that names a
     commit permanently, any other name for `REV_SHA_TTL` (15 s), and all names are dropped when the `git`
     sync token changes (`clear_revision_caches`). Caching avoids repeated `git rev-parse` subprocesses across
     tree, blob-map, and build-layout lookups.
   - `map_blob_hashes(reader, blob_shas)` joins the Git blob SHAs to `m_file_blob.blob_hash` (`blob_hash` ==
     Git blob SHA-1) and returns `{blob_sha: (blob_id, ftype)}`, preferring typed (`ftype != 0`) rows. Blobs
     absent from the map were never parsed (unindexed).
   - `blob_paths(reader, rev)` returns `{blob_id: [paths]}` for the indexed blobs of the revision's tree
     (sorted paths; one blob may sit at several paths). It is cached per commit SHA (8 entries): for
     `BLOB_PATHS_TTL` = 120 s, so blobs indexed by a running parse appear without a restart, except for the
     head commit of a ref whose ingestion finished, whose blobs are all indexed and whose map is kept until
     the parse state changes (`clear_revision_caches`). Symbol services use it to scope `m_symbol_def`
     (content-addressed by `blob_id`) to any revision; see §4 *Revision scoping of symbol queries*.
3. **Arch-Aware Definition Ranking (`definition_rank`, `best_path`, `definition_arch`)**:
   A symbol defined once per architecture (`struct pt_regs`, `setup_arch`, `thread_struct`...) resolves to the
   definition of one ARCH value: the `arch` parameter of the symbol endpoints, which the frontend sets to the
   KConfig engine's ARCH while the engine is on with a resolved configuration, and to `x86_64` otherwise
   (§5.19). `definition_arch(version, arch)` resolves the ARCH value through `KconfigService.resolve_arch`
   (unknown values fall back to `x86_64`) and returns it with its `ArchScope` and word size (`arch_bits`:
   `x86_64` → 64, `i386` → 32, generic `x86` → none). The scope is the ARCH's build layout at the revision
   (`webapp/backend/services/arch_layout_service.py`): the `m_arch_root` rows the parser stored for the
   version's head commit, or, for revisions without rows (branches, commits never ingested), the same
   evaluation of the revision's Makefiles from Git (`parser/arch_layout.py`,
   `parser/kconfig_ast/KCONFIG_API.md` §6.5), cached per (commit, ARCH); without a layout, the SRCARCH's
   `own_arch_dirs` are assumed. Definitions are ordered by:
   - prototypes (`SymbolLinkage.PrototypeDecl`) after every definition with a body;
   - path group (`path_arch_group`): the scope's own files (its architecture trees, `ArchLayout.arch_trees()`,
     and the asm-generic headers its generated wrappers include), then generic code, then the other
     `include/asm-generic/` and `include/uapi/asm-generic/` headers, then other architectures. An architecture
     tree is `arch/<a>/` or, in 2.6.x, `include/asm-<a>/` (`path_arch`): `atomic_t` at v2.6.12 resolves to
     `include/asm-x86_64/atomic.h` for x86_64 (the build links `include/asm` to it),
     `include/asm-i386/atomic.h` for i386, and ARCH=um's layout also owns `x86_64` through its
     `include/asm-um/arch` link; m68knommu at v2.6.30 owns `arch/m68k/` (hdr-arch). The same layout trees
     decide `other_arch` of the build-condition and Kconfig endpoints (`KconfigService._arch_trees`,
     `is_other_arch_path` in `parser/kbuild_conditions.py`);
   - word size: files of the other word size (`process_32.c` on x86_64, `page_64.h` on i386) after the others;
   - weak/alias definitions (`WeakOrAliasDef`) after strong ones, then path and line.
   A blob present at several paths is reported at its best-ranked path (`best_path`). Choosing between
   `#ifdef` branches of one file and between files Kbuild does not compile is done by the frontend against the
   actual configuration (§5.19).
4. **Definitions Reached From the Use Site (`from_file`)**: when the request names the file the symbol is used
   in, `SymbolService._prefer_reachable()` puts first the definitions the compilation of that file reads for
   the ARCH, i.e. what the compiler sees. `arch_layout_service.reachable(rev, arch, file)` walks the file's
   `#include` chain with the ARCH's build layout (`parser/include_graph.py`,
   `parser/kconfig_ast/KCONFIG_API.md` §6.6): forced `-include` files first, quoted names in the including
   file's directory, then the `-I` directories in order, through the build's symlinks and generated
   asm-generic wrappers. `#include` lines count whatever `#if` block holds them (the frontend still drops
   definitions its configuration compiles out), and directives come from the parser's per-blob facts
   (`m_blob_facts` family 3, `parser/include_facts.py`: the walk hands each breadth-first level to
   `IncludeResolver.reachable(prefetch=…)`, one query per level for the blobs not cached), else from Git, once
   per blob (cached by blob SHA, 50,000 entries; each walk cached per (commit, ARCH, file), 32 entries; a cold
   walk of `include/linux/sched.h` at v2.6.12 takes ~0.3 s). Reached definitions go before the path groups of
   item 3, prototypes stay last and weak definitions after strong ones; definitions are marked `visible`.
   `atomic_t` used in `include/linux/sched.h` at v2.6.12 thus resolves through
   `include/asm-x86_64/semaphore.h` to `include/asm-x86_64/atomic.h` for x86_64 (through `include/linux/sem.h`
   → `include/asm-um/atomic.h` → `include/asm-um/arch/atomic.h` = `include/asm-x86_64/atomic.h` for ARCH=um),
   and never to the unrelated `net/rxrpc/internal.h`. The walk reads the files themselves rather than
   `m_ast_include`/`m_file_reference`: those rows come from the parser's own clang run, which links
   `include/asm` to `asm-generic` and skips the includes of inactive `#if` branches, so they describe no
   particular ARCH.

### 2.8. 3-Level Semantic Cross-Version Diff Engine (`webapp/backend/services/diff_service.py`)
Either side of a comparison may be a release tag, a branch, or an arbitrary commit SHA. Comparison is
evaluated in three progressive tiers to optimize latency:
1. **Level 1 (O(1) Content Blob Filter)**: Resolves `{path: blob_sha}` for both revisions via
   `GitTreeResolver` (Path C), falling back to `{path: blob_id}` from `m_bridge_checkpoint` /
   `TreeResolverService` only when Git is unavailable on both sides. Unchanged files (equal content keys) are
   short-circuited in $O(1)$. **Renames** pair a deleted with an added path (`DiffService._pair_renames`):
   with Git trees, `git diff-tree -r -z --name-status --diff-filter=R -M50% -l1000` reports each pair with its
   content similarity (`R087` → 87); then a deleted path whose exact content reappears under a still unpaired
   added path is paired at 100 (this is the only rule without Git). Git compares contents only while `added`
   and `deleted` (after exact and same-basename pairs) each stay within the limit and their product within its
   square; beyond that it pairs only identical files and files that kept their basename and asks for a higher
   limit, which the response reports as `renames.exhaustive: false` / `renames.limit_needed`, shown in the
   Compare view's rename note (v3.0→v3.1: every pair compared, 391 renames of which 161 identical, ~0.5 s;
   v3.0→v4.0: 2,967 renames without the exhaustive pass, `limit_needed` 19,771). The exhaustive pass for such
   ranges is the separate rename search (`GET /api/tools/diff/renames`), run on request and scoped to a
   directory.
2. **Level 2 (AST & Symbol Structural Diff)**: For the first 50 modified source files (`.c`, `.h`, `.S`,
   `.rs`; paths sort documentation and dotfiles first) whose blobs are indexed on both sides, compares symbol
   definition records in `m_symbol_def` by `(name, type_id)` (one query for all of them) to surface added and
   removed definitions.
3. **Level 3 (Kconfig Scoped Diff)**: Lists added/removed/modified Kconfig source files (`Kconfig`,
   `Kconfig.*`) from the Git trees, then reads the definitions of only the files whose blob differs
   (`webapp/backend/services/kconfig_facts.py`, the cache Kconfig history shares, per blob SHA: the parser's
   stored definitions, `m_blob_facts` family 4, one query per 500 blobs; else parsed from Git with
   `parser/kconfig_ast/kconfig_definitions.py`) and compares each symbol's definitions there: properties
   (type, prompt, defaults, `depends on` including the dependencies inherited from enclosing
   `if`/`menu`/`choice` blocks, selects, implies, ranges, choice, options, `transitional`, help) per defining
   file. A definition that only moved lines is unchanged. A symbol is added/removed only when no Kconfig file
   of the other revision defines it (files with the same blob on both sides are checked with one `git grep`).
   Without Git trees (revisions Git cannot resolve), the indexed versions' Kconfig tags are compared instead
   (name -> set of definition text hashes, `DiffService._fetch_kconfig_symbols`).

### 2.9. Git-Native Database Architecture & Commit Hash Formatting
1. **Zero-VID Native Table Queries & Elimination of View Dependencies**:
   All webapp backend routers and services operate directly on Git-native content-addressable relational
   tables, completely bypassing legacy SQL compatibility views (`m_v_main`, `m_file`, `m_bridge_file`,
   `m_bridge_commit_file`):
   - Version catalog and resolution query `m_git_ref` joined with `m_commit`.
   - Filesystem tree and directory hierarchies list the Git tree of the requested revision (`GitTreeResolver`,
     Path C) and annotate files with `blob_id`/`ftype` from `m_file_blob` via the content-addressed
     `blob_hash`, so tags, branches, and intermediate commits all return their complete file list. Without a
     Git repository, they fall back to `m_checkpoint_tree` and `TreeResolverService`.
   - The code view (`get_file`) resolves a file's indexed blob from `m_checkpoint_tree`, or—for non-checkpoint
     commits—from the Git blob SHA returned by `git cat-file`, joined to `m_file_blob.blob_hash`.
   - Cross-version and file diffing use Git trees (Path C) with `m_file_blob` blob-hash annotation, falling
     back to `m_checkpoint_tree` and `TreeResolverService.resolve_tree`. Every reader of a version's tree goes
     through that view; only `history_service` looks blobs up in `m_bridge_checkpoint` directly (by `blob_id`,
     which a delta version's own rows or its base's hold).
   - Preprocessor `#include` resolution leverages compiler-verified `m_file_reference` (`ref_type=1`)
     provenance.
   - Backward-compatible JSON field mappings (`vid` = `commit_id`, `fid` = `blob_id`) are preserved so all
     frontend clients continue functioning seamlessly.
2. **Commit Hash Formatting (`format_commit_hash`)**:
   `m_commit.commit_hash` stores 20-byte binary Git SHA-1 digests (`BINARY(20)`). Backend services
   (`git_service.py`, `helpers.py`) format binary hashes using `format_commit_hash(val)` / `hash_hex(val)`
   (`bytes(val).hex()`; a `str` that mysql-connector returned for a hash whose bytes happen to be valid UTF-8
   is re-encoded to its 20 bytes first), ensuring 40-character lowercase hexadecimal strings in all JSON API
   responses. API endpoints support both 40-character hexadecimal queries (using SQL `UNHEX(%s)`), short
   commit hash prefixes, and legacy integer `commit_id` values.

---

### 2.10. Multi-Repository Request Scoping (`webapp/backend/config.py`, `webapp/backend/security/middleware.py`)
1. **Repository selection**: `RepoContextMiddleware` (pure ASGI, outermost) reads the `X-KI-Repo` header or
   `?repo=` query parameter and stores the matching configured repository (core config `"repositories"`, see
   `core/API.md` §7.1.1) in a `ContextVar`. Unknown or missing names fall back to the default repository.
   Because it is pure ASGI, sync endpoints running in the threadpool inherit the value.
2. **Git access**: Every service resolves the work tree through `get_repo_dir()`; `git_reader` is a
   `GitReaderPool` with up to 4 persistent `git cat-file --batch` processes per repository, and
   `GitTreeResolver.repo_dir` follows the request unless pinned.
3. **Database scoping**: `get_active_repo_id(reader)` maps the repository to `m_repository.repo_id` (by name,
   then `git_url`; `-1` when never parsed). Version resolution (`get_version_info`) and the version/branch
   catalogs only consider that repository's `m_git_ref` rows. Commit ids, blobs and tags are global and need
   no scoping.
4. **Caches**: Module caches keyed by version names (`_INCLUDE_CACHE`, `_TREEMAP_CACHE`, `_MAINTAINER_CACHE`,
   `_FILE_SUBSYSTEMS_CACHE`, `_CREDITS_KEYS_CACHE`, the Kconfig `_MODELS` / `_LISTING_CACHE` / `_PATHS_CACHE`
   / `_USAGE_CACHE` / `_BUILD_RESOLVERS`, version name/id caches) or by content (`_FILE_TOKENS_CACHE` per
   blob, `_BLOB_SECTIONS_CACHE` / `_BLOB_CREDITS_CACHE` per MAINTAINERS / CREDITS blob, `_ARCH_INFO_CACHE` per
   commit and ARCH) are `RepoScopedCache` instances that transparently prefix keys with the repository name;
   the git file-history LRU cache takes the repository path as an argument. A cache keyed by a version name
   would keep answering for the commit a branch pointed at, so all of them are cleared when the `parsed`
   **or** the `git` sync token changes (§2.11).
   A `RepoScopedCache` takes an optional `maxsize` and then evicts the least recently used entry. Every cache
   whose key carries a request parameter is bounded, because otherwise each distinct value a caller sends adds
   an entry that is never released: `_INCLUDE_CACHE` (4096; keyed by header and referring file),
   `_FILE_TOKENS_CACHE` (512), `_TREEMAP_CACHE` (64; each entry is a whole subtree), `_FILE_SUBSYSTEMS_CACHE`
   (4096; keyed by file path), `_MAINTAINER_CACHE` (16; one MAINTAINERS model per version, and any commit SHA
   is a version), `_CREDITS_KEYS_CACHE` (16), the version name/id maps (`_NAME_TO_VID_CACHE`,
   `_VID_TO_NAME_CACHE`, 50,000 each; a separate `_PRELOADED` flag records that the repository's refs were
   loaded), `_USAGE_CACHE` (256; keyed by Kconfig symbol), `_LISTING_CACHE` (64; keyed by revision),
   `_ARCH_INFO_CACHE` (256) and `_PATHS_CACHE` (4, separate because one entry is a revision's whole file list:
   36,783 paths / ~4.5 MiB at v3.0, more in later releases). A failed or timed-out `git` call of the Kconfig
   service is never cached as an empty answer. Caches keyed only by what the repository itself defines stay
   unbounded, and the callers that evict by their own policy (`_MODELS`, `_BUILD_RESOLVERS`) reach through
   `dict.pop` and are unaffected. Because a bounded cache can evict between a membership test and a read, its
   callers read once into a local (`.get()`) rather than testing and then indexing.
5. **Unparsed repositories** remain browsable: tags absent from `m_git_ref` resolve through `git rev-parse` to
   `vid = 0`, and trees, files, searches, diffs and treemaps read Git directly.
6. **Projects**: an entry's project slug (`repository_project_slug()`: its `project`, else `man-pages` for a
   Linux man-pages clone recognised by `core.config.is_manpages_repository()`, else `linux`) is listed by
   `GET /api/projects` as `project`; `is_manpages_entry()` tells the man-pages entry. A man-pages entry without
   configured `tag_views` gets `core.config.MANPAGES_TAG_VIEWS` (one view grouping `man-pages-X.*` by major).
   The Git-only tags of every project other than `linux` are listed in release order
   (`versions.release_tag_key()` over `parser/git_ast/release_order.py`, any `<prefix>X.Y[.Z][-rcN]` scheme:
   `man-pages-6.0-rc1` < `man-pages-6.00` < `man-pages-6.04` < `man-pages-6.04.01` < `man-pages-6.7`; a name with
   a release prefix that does not parse, `man-pages-6.05-a1`, just before that release); `linux` keeps git's
   version sort.
7. **Another repository within a request**: a service that answers from a second configured repository (the
   man-pages repository from a kernel request and back, §2.20) runs that part inside
   `man_service.using_repo(name)`, which sets the request's repository `ContextVar` for the block and resets it
   afterwards, so `get_repo_dir()`, the Git reader pool, `git_tree_resolver` and `RepoScopedCache` keys all
   follow the other repository.

### 2.11. Client Synchronization & Build-Bound Assets (`webapp/backend/services/sync_service.py`, `webapp/frontend/js/sync.js`)
Clients must follow server changes without the user knowing to reload. The server keeps five change tokens
(12-hex digests, cached so most requests cost no database or Git work):
| Token | Covers | Computed from (cache) | Client reaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `db` | Database rebuilt | `m_db_instance` (30 s) | Every cached API response is dropped |
| `frontend` | Webapp code changed | SHA-256 of the files under `webapp/frontend/` (path + content; the JS unit tests in `webapp/frontend/tests/` are left out and never served), recomputed only when a file's size, mtime, ctime or inode changed (checked every 5 s); identical files give the same build across restarts | The page reloads into the new build (see below) |
| `parsed` | Versions of the active repository finished, re-parsed or rolled back | `m_git_ref` + `m_ingest_state` of the repository, unfinished versions excluded (15 s) | Version/branch lists are refetched; cached data of versions whose stamp changed is dropped. On the server, a change also clears the per-version caches (`clear_parse_dependent_caches()`: version-name maps, file tokens, include resolution, maintainers, history facts, blob-path maps) |
| `git` | Tags fetched, branches moved | `git for-each-ref` of the repository (15 s) | Same as `parsed`, server side included: caches keyed by a revision name (a branch's file tokens, Kconfig model, maintainers, name → commit) are cleared, and the revision → SHA and blob-map caches of `GitTreeResolver` (`clear_revision_caches`; tree listings are content-addressed and kept) |
| `projects` | Repository list changed: a repository added or removed, parsed for the first time, its clone gone, its configuration changed | `projects_catalog()` (configured repositories + `m_repository`/`m_project`, what `GET /api/projects` lists without the request's `active` flag) (30 s) | The repository list is refetched and the selectors re-rendered (`projects:updated`); it is not refetched with `parsed`/`git` changes |
- **Delivery**: `GET /api/sync` returns all five. `SyncHeaderMiddleware` (inside `RepoContextMiddleware`, so
  tokens are those of the request's repository) adds `X-KIP-Sync: <db>.<parsed>.<git>` to every `/api/`
  response, so any request reveals a change without polling (`projects` is not in the header: the `GET
  /api/sync` checks below reveal it). While the three tokens are cached the header is read in place
  (`cached_header_value`); only a refresh goes to the threadpool, and one refresh per token runs at a time
  (`_Ttl`: requests arriving meanwhile wait for its answer instead of each running `git for-each-ref` or the
  database query).
- **When clients check**: clients synchronize with the server (`GET /api/sync`) when the page opens
  (`syncManager.start()`), when opening a new tab (`tab:opened`), when restoring a workspace session
  (`session:adopted`/`session:restored`), and periodically every **60 s** via the reachability heartbeat
  (`pingServer()`), in addition to following `X-KIP-Sync` headers on all other API responses. Every sync check
  inspects all tokens (`frontend`, `db`, `parsed`, `git`, `projects`): a newer frontend build prompts an
  update banner immediately (no hourly delay; "Later" postpones it for the current session), a changed `db`
  purges caches, changed `parsed`/`git` tokens refresh the version and branch catalogs and their stamps, and a
  changed `projects` token refreshes the repository list (`syncManager.refreshProjects()`). Version, branch,
  and project catalogs are served cache-first from IndexedDB on refresh without hitting the network until a
  sync confirmation signals that those catalogs must be refetched.
- **Manual check** (`syncManager.checkNow()`, Settings popover **🔄 Check for Updates**, §5.5): the same sync
  as the 60 s heartbeat, run at once: `GET /api/sync` (the server's cached tokens, no `fresh`), applied by the
  same `apply()`, so a changed `db` purges the caches, changed `parsed`/`git` tokens refetch the catalogs and
  stamps and a changed `projects` token the repository list, and nothing is refetched when no token changed.
  Two differences: nothing is re-rendered in place and a newer build is not announced (`apply(…, {notify:
  false, announce: false})`), because an update found **restarts the page at once** (`syncManager.restart()`):
  into the new build when the frontend changed (`reloadToLatest()`, cached shell dropped, even after
  **Later**), otherwise a plain reload whose shell and modules still come from the Service Worker. An update
  is a frontend build other than the running page's, a token changed since the last sync, or a version whose
  stamp changed. Resolves to `{db, parsed, git, projects, frontend, newBuild, changed, removed, added,
  updated}`. What was found is kept in `sessionStorage["kip-restart-note"]` and toasted by the restarted page
  (*Updates applied: …*, `syncManager.takeRestartNote()`); with no update the popover reports *Up to date*. It
  compares against the server's local Git repository; it does not `git fetch` from a remote.
- **Version stamps**: `/api/versions` and `/api/branches` give each version a `stamp` (`<commit
  sha[:12]>.<parse completion time>`, `.0` for versions parsed before `m_ingest_state`, `.git` when not
  parsed; a branch uses its current Git head). `api._vk(version)` puts `"<name>@<stamp>~"` into every
  version-scoped cache key, so a re-parsed version or a moved branch never serves older cached data;
  `syncManager.refreshVersions()` deletes the entries of versions whose stamp changed
  (`localDB.deleteDataWhere`, `isStaleKey`) and emits `versions:updated` (`{changed, removed, added,
  newlyIndexed}`); `app.js` then rebuilds the selectors, toasts newly indexed versions and re-renders open
  views of changed versions. The watch list (§5.36) listens too: watches following a branch that moved are
  checked. A change of cache-key layout (`CACHE_LAYOUT`) clears the data stores once.
- **Build-bound assets**: `GET /` renders `index.html` with `__KIP_BUILD__` replaced by the current build
  (`<meta name="kip-build">`) and every `"/static/` URL rewritten to `"/b/<build>/` (`render_index()`);
  relative ES-module imports inherit the prefix. `GET /b/{build}/{path}` serves the current build's files with
  `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` and answers **409** for any other build, so a page
  never mixes modules of two builds. The shell and `/boot.js` are sent with `Cache-Control: private,
  max-age=3600`, `sw.js` with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` (registered with
  `updateViaCache: "all"` so refreshes never poll `sw.js`, and updated via `fetch(..., {cache: "reload"})` +
  `reg.update()` only when `GET /api/sync` reveals a build change). Legacy `/static/`, `/js/`, `/css/` mounts
  stay for direct access. `js/theme_boot.js` (G08) is a classic, render-blocking script in `<head>` (external,
  as the CSP requires) that sets `data-theme` from `localStorage` before the stylesheets paint, so a light
  theme never flashes dark.
- **`boot.js`** (classic external script, the CSP forbids inline ones): sets `window.KIP_BUILD` and imports
  the build's `app.js` (`data-entry`). If the import fails (409: the cached shell is older than the server's
  build and its modules are not cached), it deletes the `kip-shell`/`kip-assets` caches and reloads once
  (`sessionStorage["kip-stale-build-reload"]` prevents a loop; a second failure shows an error box).
  `window.KIP_RELOAD_TO_LATEST()` does the same on request. `app.js` starts on `DOMContentLoaded`, or
  immediately when the import resolves after it.
- **Service worker** (`sw.js`): `kip-shell` holds `/` (every shell path and query share one entry) and
  `/boot.js`, cache-first; `kip-assets` holds `/b/<build>/…`, cache-first (the page posts `{type: "prune",
  build}` on start to drop other builds); `kip-api` holds API responses, network-first with cache fallback
  (`/api/sync` is never cached, so it always reaches the server), bounded to `API_CACHE_LIMIT` (300) entries,
  oldest dropped first; replies marked `Cache-Control: no-store` (version catalog deltas, §2.13) are passed
  through without being stored. A reply the worker serves from `kip-api` after the request failed, and its
  synthesized `503`, carry `X-KIP-Offline: 1`, so the page does not mistake a cached reply for a live one
  (§5.1 *Server reachability*). Caches not named `kip-*` (e.g. the former `kernel-ide-v10`) are deleted on
  activation; there is no hand-maintained pre-cache list.
- **New build announcement** (`syncManager.announceUpdate()`): a bottom banner *"KernelInfo was updated (build
  …). Reloading in 5 s…"* with **Reload now** and **Later**; the countdown waits while a dialog
  (`.ki-modal-backdrop`) is open. Reloading drops the cached shell first, so the next page is the new build;
  tabs and KConfig profiles survive (saved in `localStorage`). **Later** dismisses it for the current session
  until a newer build appears; a manual check restarts into the build regardless.

### 2.12. Startup Catalog Warm-Up (`webapp/backend/app.py:lifespan`, `webapp/backend/routers/versions.py`)
A restarted server has empty in-memory caches, and a client after **Full Local Reset** (§5.5) has an empty
IndexedDB, so the first page load would otherwise pay for every catalog itself — above all the branch-tags
walk (`GET /api/branch/tags`, ~18 s for `master` of Linux).
- **What runs**: after the database pool is pre-warmed, `lifespan` starts `start_prewarm()`, a daemon thread
  (`kip-prewarm`) that does not delay startup. For every configured repository whose work tree exists it
  selects that repository (`set_active_repository`), reads `get_versions(include_rc=True)` and
  `get_branches()` (building the cached version and branch catalogs, §2.13, and warming the database pool, Git
  packs and the OS page cache) and walks the tags of the branch marked `is_default`, filling
  `_BRANCH_TAGS_CACHE`. It logs `Pre-warmed <repo> in <s> s (default branch <name>: <n> tags)` at INFO; a
  failure is logged as a warning and never stops the server.
- **Shared walks**: `branch_tags(head)` keeps one in-flight walk per `(repository, head)`
  (`_BRANCH_TAGS_INFLIGHT`), so a request arriving while the warm-up still walks `master` waits for that walk
  instead of starting a second `git for-each-ref --merged` (it is answered when the warm-up finishes, not 18 s
  after it arrived). The walk uses the resolved head, so a branch moving during it cannot mix two positions. A
  failed or timed-out walk (180 s) is not cached.
- **Shutdown**: `cancel_branch_walks()` terminates walks still running, so a `--reload` restart does not leave
  Git processes behind.
- Only the default branch is warmed; another branch is walked on its first request and then cached as before.

### 2.13. Catalog Caching & Compact Version Catalog (`webapp/backend/services/catalog_cache.py`, `webapp/backend/routers/versions.py`, `webapp/frontend/js/utils/version_catalog.js`)
The version catalog is the largest response clients refetch: ~5,800 Linux tags (988 KB of JSON, 218 KB
gzipped), and every client refetched it whenever the `parsed` token changed (§2.11), i.e. each time the parser
finished a version (every ~2 minutes during a run). Building it took ~0.6 s of database, `git for-each-ref`
and JSON/gzip work per request.
- **Built once per repository state** (`TokenCache`): `/api/versions` and `/api/branches` only change with the
  active repository's `parsed` or `git` token, so each is built once per token pair (keyed by repository, and
  `include_rc` for versions) and served from memory until a token changes; requests arriving during a build
  wait for it (one build per key). A token that could not be computed (`""`) only vouches for a value for 15
  s. A rebuild whose content is unchanged (e.g. only a remote branch moved) keeps the previous catalog and its
  encodings.
- **Pre-encoded bodies** (`JsonBody`): the JSON (rendered exactly as `JSONResponse` does) and its gzip (level
  9) are encoded once per catalog, not per request; `respond()` sends the gzip bytes with `Content-Encoding:
  gzip` when the request accepts it (`GZipMiddleware` passes encoded bodies through) and adds `Vary:
  Accept-Encoding, X-KI-Repo`.
- **ETag / 304**: catalog responses carry a weak `ETag` (a content digest) and `Cache-Control: no-cache`, so
  the browser keeps them and revalidates; a request whose `If-None-Match` names the current ETag (or `*`) gets
  `304` without a body. The browser does this by itself for `/api/branches` (and the legacy `/api/versions`
  layout).
- **Compact version catalog** (`GET /api/versions?compact=1`, §4.1, what the frontend reads): positional
  columns without the fields the client can derive — `indexed` (a parse time is present), `is_prerelease` (the
  name), the `stamp` (`<sha12>.<parse time>` / `<sha12>.git`, identical to the legacy one, so no cached data
  is invalidated) — and with 12-hex commits instead of 40, `vid` left out (no view reads it): 183 KB raw / 67
  KB gzipped instead of 988 KB / 218 KB. Its ETag is `W/"c1-<g>"`, `g` being the generation (digest of the
  catalog content) and `c1` the layout version.
- **Deltas**: the server keeps the compact rows of the last 64 generations per repository and `include_rc`
  (`_HISTORY`, unchanged rows shared between generations). A client sending `If-None-Match: W/"c1-<g>"` for a
  generation it holds receives `304` when nothing changed, else only the operations turning its generation
  into the current one (`{g, b, d}`, ~110 bytes for a version that finished parsing; `Cache-Control:
  no-store`, no ETag), computed once per base generation. An unknown generation (older than the history,
  another server process, a restart) or a delta not smaller than the full catalog gets the full catalog.
- **Client** (`api.getVersions()`, §5.1): the catalog is kept in IndexedDB as `{g, r}` (`files` store, key
  `<repo>::app_versions_c1_<rc|rel>`) and decoded once per generation in memory; the sync refresh (§2.11)
  sends the generation it holds and applies the 304, delta or full answer. The Service Worker does not store
  `no-store` replies, so a delta never stands in for the catalog offline.

### 2.14. Disk Cache of Derived Data (`webapp/backend/services/disk_cache.py`)
Expensive results computed from Git (Kconfig models, commit relation and release indexes, Kbuild object
indexes, reports) survive server restarts as gzipped JSON files. This cache lives **outside the database**,
which the webapp never writes (§2.5), exactly as the Kconfig model cache always did.
- **API**: `DiskCache(namespace, max_bytes=256 MiB, max_entries=None)` with `get(key)`, `put(key, obj)`
  (atomic: a per-process temporary file, then `os.replace`; never raises, returns success), `delete(key)`,
  `entries()`, `size_bytes()`; `fingerprint(*paths, salt=)` / `module_fingerprint(*repo_relative_files,
  salt=)` hash the source files that shape a result (once per process); `usage()` lists every namespace's size
  (status page, §5.37).
- **Location**: `cache_engine.cache_root()` (`KERNELINFO_CACHE_DIR`, else config `cache.dir`, else
  `~/.cache/kernelinfo`), one directory per namespace
  (`kconfig-models`, `commit-relations`, …). Keys are hashed into file names (`<sha1>.json.gz`), except keys
  that already are a hex digest, so the Kconfig model files written before the helper existed are still found.
- **Eviction**: least recently used by file mtime (refreshed on every read) when a namespace exceeds its
  `max_bytes` or `max_entries`, and across namespaces when the total exceeds `webapp.cache.max_mb` (default
  1024, §7.1).
- **Binary entries**: `BinaryDiskCache(namespace, ...)` holds raw bytes (`get_bytes(key)` / `put_bytes(key,
  data)`, files `<key>.bin`) under the same eviction and global cap; the source index keeps its assembled
  revisions there (§2.19).
- **Rules for callers**: a key includes the repository name and the fingerprint of the producing code;
  failures, partial and timed-out results are never stored.
- **Indexed side-stores** (commit relations, release index, source-index fact stores, Kernel API records) are not
  gzip files: they are record stores too large or too query-shaped for a JSON blob, kept through the pluggable
  `cache_engine` (`cache_engine/CACHE_API.md`; `get_cache_engine()`, engine chosen by config `cache.engine`, default
  `"ram"`, also `"sqlite"`; the same cache root). Services declare `StoreSpec`s and never touch a storage driver: no `import
  sqlite3` in `webapp/`. A space is named `<repository>-v<format>` (or `<family>-v<format>`); a layout change bumps the
  format, which rebuilds. Cache failures surface as `cache_engine.CacheError`.

### 2.15. Background Jobs and 202 Responses (`webapp/backend/services/jobs.py`, `webapp/frontend/js/utils/job_poll.js`)
Work that takes seconds to minutes runs on a small pool of daemon worker threads instead of holding an HTTP
request open.
- **Backend**: `jobs.submit(key, fn, cache=None, cache_key=None)` starts `fn(progress)` unless a job with that
  key is already queued, running or done (one job per key: concurrent submissions share it) and returns its
  state `{key, state: "building" | "done" | "failed", progress: {done, total, note}, started_at, finished_at,
  result?, error?}`; `jobs.get(key)`, `jobs.wait(key, timeout)`, `jobs.run_sync(key, fn, …, timeout)`
  (in-process callers), `jobs.cancel(key)`, `jobs.stats()`. A disk-cache hit (§2.14) answers without starting
  a job.
- **Workers**: `webapp.jobs.workers` (default 2) daemon threads per process; queued jobs report `progress.note
  = "queued"`. A job runs in a copy of the submitting request's context, so the active repository (§2.10) is
  the one of the request that started it.
- **Progress and cancellation**: `progress(done, total, note)` updates the state and raises `JobCancelled`
  once the job is cancelled; `progress.cancelled` is the `threading.Event` long subprocess loops check
  themselves. `cancel_all()` runs from the `lifespan` shutdown next to `cancel_branch_walks()` (§2.12).
- **Results**: written to the disk cache when one is given, and kept in an in-memory LRU of 16 results.
  Failures are logged and kept for 60 s (pollers see `failed` with its message), never cached; a later
  submission after that retries.
- **HTTP convention** (`respond_job(key, fn, cache=, cache_key=, wait=0, shape=None)` keeps routers to one
  line): the result ready (cache or memory) → `200` with the body (`shape(result)` when given); not ready →
  `202 Accepted`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, body `{state: "building", key, progress, retry_after_ms}`; failed
  → `500 {"detail": "background job failed: …"}`. `wait` lets a cheap job answer within the same request.
- **Frontend**: `api.requestJob(endpoint, {onProgress, signal, cacheStore, cacheKey, method, body})` repeats
  the request while it answers 202, with a backoff from 500 ms doubling to 5 s (the server's `retry_after_ms`
  can only lengthen it; `nextJobDelay`), calls `onProgress({done, total, note})`, and stops with an
  `AbortError` when `signal` (the view's `AbortController`, aborted on `dispose()` or when the tab closes)
  fires. Only the final body is stored in IndexedDB; the Service Worker keeps only `200` replies (§2.11), so a
  202 is never served offline. `progressLabel()` / `progressFraction()` format the progress for a view.

### 2.16. Commit Relations (`webapp/backend/services/commit_relations.py`)
"Which commits refer to this commit, and how?", from two sources:
- **Database first**: the parser stores what every commit message it ingests names (`m_commit_relation`,
  `m_commit_link`, `core/API.md` §4 rows 63-64; older commits by `--backfill-commit-relations`, §12). Once the
  backfill state row says `done:` (`db_ready()`, a negative answer rechecked after 60 s), a commit in the
  active network's `m_commit` is answered there (`db_relations()`, `source: "db"`, `SELECT` only): forward
  rows by `commit_id`, reverse lists (`fixed_by`, `reverted_by`, `backports`) through `commit_rel_target_idx`
  — the stored target, or an unresolved prefix of the commit (zero `target_hash`) — subjects and dates of
  related commits from `m_commit`, else Git (`git log --no-walk`), `Fixes:` targets left unresolved at
  ingestion resolved as below. Same shape, `LIST_CAP` and `<list>_total` as the index. `db_counts()` (timeline
  chips, batched), `db_fixes_of()`, `db_backports_of()`, `db_commits_for_mids()` (§4.8). **Coverage**: reverse
  lists only hold commits the parser ingested; fixes and backports made only on refs never ingested (e.g.
  linux-next, stable series never parsed) are missing until ingested. Readers that need complete reverse lists
  over some releases check `tags_ingested(tags)`: every commit of those release segments (`m_commit_release`,
  §2.17) is in `m_commit` (the CVE context's backports, the stable-missing report). `relations_token()` (in
  report cache keys) changes with either source.
- **Relation index** (cache_engine space, below): commits the database does not hold (refs never ingested), and everything
  while the backfill has not finished. It is built only when such a lookup misses the database, never at
  startup; a repository the database covers never builds it. It reads every commit of every ref, so git-only
  versions, stable branches and commits past the parser's ingestion caps are covered.
- **Relations** (`parse_relations`, pure, in `parser/git_ast/commit_relations.py` and re-exported here):
  `Fixes: <hex 8–40> ("subject")` → *fixes* / *fixed by* (the target is an abbreviation, resolved lazily with
  `git rev-parse --verify --quiet <hex>^{commit}`, the suffix appended on the server to a validated hex
  string, results cached; an unknown or ambiguous prefix keeps its quoted subject); `This reverts commit
  <sha>.` → *reverts* / *reverted by*; `commit <sha> upstream.`, `[ Upstream commit <sha> ]`, `(cherry picked
  from commit <sha>)` → *upstream* / *backports*; `Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 3.0+` → *stable_cc* with its
  annotation; `Link:` (lore.kernel.org, lkml.kernel.org/r, patch.msgid.link) and `Message-Id:` → message-ids
  (unbracketed, URL-decoded, lower-cased, as in §5.26). Lines must start the line: a `Fixes` word in prose or
  a quoted `> commit … upstream.` is not a relation. A revert or backport naming an abbreviated hash keeps it
  as a prefix (resolved like `Fixes:` targets).
- **Build**: two `git log --all` passes run in parallel — trailers only
  (`%(trailers:key=Fixes,key=Cc,key=Link,key=Message-Id)`) for commits matching `^Fixes:`, `^Cc:.*stable@`,
  `^Link:`, `^Message-Id:`, and bodies for reverts and backports — streamed into a cache_engine space
  (`commit-relations`, `<repository>-v<format>`; stores `commits`, `rel`, `links`; SQLite engine: file
  `commit-relations/<repository>-v<format>.sqlite3` under the cache root, §2.14) in a background job (§2.15), one
  `batch()` per write. On the
  reference Linux clone with its stable branches: 1.49 M commits read in ~270 s, 1.08 M commits, 1.68 M
  relations and 626 k mail links stored (~570 MB). Lookups take 1–50 ms.
- **Refresh**: the store records the ref heads it covered. When the `git` token changes (§2.11,
  `register_refs_changed`), the next request reads only the new commits (`git log --stdin` with the new heads
  and `^` the covered ones) while the existing store keeps answering (`refreshing: true`, sent `no-store`).
  The store is versioned by `INDEX_FORMAT`, not by the module's source, so editing the code does not throw
  away a 4-minute build.
- **API** (in process): `relations(sha)` → `{fixes, fixed_by, reverts, reverted_by, upstream, backports,
  stable_cc, links}` (each related commit with its subject and date; lists longer than 100 keep the most
  recent ones and report `<list>_total` — `Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4` alone is cited by 6,336 commits),
  `commits_for_mid(mid)`, `status()`. While the first build runs, `relations()` answers `{state: "building",
  progress}` and the endpoints answer 202.
- **Operator note**: `git commit-graph write --reachable` on the served clone speeds up every walk; the webapp
  never writes to the repository.

### 2.17. Release Index (`webapp/backend/services/release_service.py`)
Shared answers about releases, from Git:
- **Ordering** (`release_key`, `parse_tag`; with `previous_in`, `final_of`, `series_name`, `family_of`,
  `release_ranges`, `release_tag_names` they live in `parser/git_ast/release_order.py`, shared with the parser's
  release statistics step, `core/API.md` §10, and re-exported here): release candidates sort before their
  release, a release before its stable updates (`v3.0 < v3.0.1 < v3.1-rc1 < v3.1-rc10 < v3.1 < v3.1.1`); v2.6.x
  releases are series `2.6.x` with the fourth number as the stable update. Only tags of commits are releases
  (`v2.6.11` tags a tree; history starts at `v2.6.12-rc2`).
- **Every project** (the request's repository, `X-KI-Repo`): `tag_commits()` keeps `release_tag_names()` of the
  repository's tags — the kernel scheme's (`vX.Y…`, `next-YYYYMMDD`) when it has any, else every
  `<prefix>X.Y[.Z][-rcN]` release (`man-pages-6.9`, `foo-1.2.3`), the prefix being the tag's family with chains
  of its own (`parser/git_ast/GIT_API.md` §7). A man-pages or any other tagged repository therefore has a
  release index, release statistics and release reports like the kernel; the cache index's ranges come from
  `release_ranges()` (the previous tag of each chain), as the parser's.
- **Previous release** (`previous`): `v3.1 → v3.0`, `v3.1-rc1 → v3.0`, `v3.1-rc2 → v3.1-rc1`, `v3.0.5 →
  v3.0.4`, `v3.0.1 → v3.0`, `v2.6.39 → v2.6.38`; `range_of(tag)` gives the commit range `(previous, tag)`.
- **Release membership from the database** (`release_lookup(shas)`, `db_lookup`, `db_covers_all`): the
  parser's release statistics store every commit of every release segment in `m_commit_release` (`core/API.md`
  §10), the first segment of each chain winning. When every tag of `tag_commits()` has a segment with its
  current commit in the current format (`db_covers_all()`, cached until the `git`/`parsed` token changes, a
  negative answer for 60 s), lookups read it (500 SHAs per query, a row counts only when its segment's tag
  still names the same commit) and a SHA without a row is on no release chain; `ensure_release_index()` then
  answers `done` without building the cache index. When it does not (tags fetched since the last parse, an
  older database), the cache index below answers once current, and until then the database rows that exist.
  `release_token()` (in report cache keys) changes with either source. `walk_segments(from_tag, to_tag)`
  follows `base_tag` from `to_tag`'s segment to `from_tag` (≤ 200 segments, `None` when not reached or a
  segment is stale) and `segment_commits(ids)` lists their commits. `first_containing()`,
  `commit_facts.release_badges()` (one batched lookup) and the CVE report context (`cve_service.Context`) read
  `release_lookup()`; the stable-missing report (§4.10) reads `m_commit_release` when the database covers its
  series, else reads the relation and release cache spaces together (`ensure_release_index(require_sqlite=True)`; the report
  uses `relation_index.space()` / `release_index.space()` and never opens a cache file itself).
- **First containing tag** (`first_containing(sha)`): `git describe --contains` costs ~14 s per commit on a
  clone without a commit-graph, so (without database coverage) an index maps every commit to the first
  mainline tag introducing it (one `git rev-list <tag> ^<previous>` per consecutive pair of the mainline
  chain) and to the first stable tag of its series. It lives in the cache engine
  (cache_engine space `release-index`, `<repository>-v<format>`; stores `tags`, `first_tag`), built by a background job (5,761 ranges in ~125 s, 66 MB)
  and extended incrementally when tags are fetched (0.2 s when nothing is new). A lookup takes a few
  milliseconds. The answer is `{first_tag, first_release (the release a candidate leads to, once tagged),
  first_stable, released}`; a commit on no release chain answers `released: false` with up to 20 branches
  containing it. Answers with a tag are cached permanently.
- **Per-release passes**: `release_commits(tag)` (`git log --no-merges <prev>..<tag>`: author, committer,
  date, subject, contributor trailers via `git_commit_parser.iter_trailers` / `CommitRole` — the parser's own
  reading, so name-less and bare-address trailers count as in `m_bridge_commit_person`; `PASS_FORMAT` 3 —
  files) and `merges(tag)` (`--first-parent --merges`: parents, subject, body, committer), background jobs
  cached on disk per (repository, range): immutable.

### 2.18. Running Repository Scripts (`webapp/backend/services/checkpatch_service.py`)
The only script the webapp runs from the tracked repository is `scripts/checkpatch.pl` (P4), and only under
these rules — a branch or commit could carry a modified copy:
- **Off by default**: `webapp.tools.checkpatch.enabled` (`false`); while off, `POST /api/tools/{v}/checkpatch`
  answers `{enabled: false, config_key, reason}` and no process is spawned.
- **Trusted source**: the script comes from `webapp.tools.checkpatch.ref` — `"latest-release"` (the newest
  final `vX.Y` tag) or an explicit release tag (`vX.Y` / `vX.Y.Z`); branches, SHAs, release candidates and the
  caller's revision are refused. It is read as `refs/tags/<tag>:scripts/checkpatch.pl` with
  `scripts/spelling.txt` and `scripts/const_structs.checkpatch` (the data files it reads;
  `Documentation/…/checkpatch.rst` only with `--verbose`, which is not used).
- **Isolation**: the files are written to a fresh temporary directory, which is the working directory and
  `$HOME` (no user `.checkpatch.conf`), removed afterwards; `perl checkpatch.pl --no-tree --terse --no-summary
  [--show-types] [--color=never]` (flags the version supports) with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`, `LANG=C.UTF-8`, a 30
  s timeout, `RLIMIT_CPU` 30 s, `RLIMIT_AS` 1 GB, `RLIMIT_NOFILE` 64 and a new session. `webapp.tools.sandbox`
  may name a wrapper: `bwrap` gets `--unshare-all` (no network), read-only system directories and only the
  temporary directory writable; any other value is prefixed as given.
- **Bounds**: patches up to 2 MB; one run at a time per process (503 *checkpatch busy* after 5 s).

### 2.19. Source Index (`webapp/backend/services/source_index.py`, `parser/source_facts.py`)
What every function of a revision calls, and what its ops tables hold. The call path finder (N2) and the ops
implementations (N1, §4.7) answer from it in memory. It is content-addressed by Git blob SHA, so it covers
every revision, git-only ones included. Reading whole call graphs from the parser's symbol rows would cost
~12–35 s per 500 files (random reads across `m_tag_ref` / `m_blob_symbol`); the parser stores compact per-blob
facts instead (`m_blob_facts`, Step 6.9, `core/API.md` §6).
- **Facts per blob** (`parser/source_facts.py` `extract(text)`, pure, shared by the parser and the webapp):
  comments, strings and character literals are blanked; preprocessor lines set aside (a `#define` body gives
  the macro's calls; constant macros calling nothing are dropped); `#if` branches restart at the brace depth
  of their `#if`, so a head written twice under `#ifdef`/`#else` does not unbalance the file. Gives `d`
  (functions with lines and `static`, function-like and object-like macros), `c` (direct calls `name(` per
  definition, without keywords, `sizeof`, type names written like calls), `m` (calls through a member,
  `->field(` / `.field(`) and `t` (`struct S name[…] [attrs] = { … }` initializers: designated `.field =
  ident` / `= &ident` entries, arrays of structs, one nested level as `outer.inner`, positional entries
  counted). Function heads are found at brace depth 0: the identifier before the last parameter list, skipping
  annotations (`__acquires(x)`), with `SYSCALL_DEFINEn(open, …)` → `sys_open`, `COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINEn` →
  `compat_sys_…` and `BPF_CALL_n(name, …)`. Not seen: calls produced by macro expansion (the macro is the
  callee and its body the next hop), other macro-defined functions, calls through a function pointer held in a
  variable.
- **Where facts come from**: first the parser's `m_blob_facts` rows of family 1 (current `FACTS_FORMAT`; every
  `.c`/`.h` blob of every ingested version, extracted by the parser once per blob, ~400 bytes each); a
  revision of an ingested version therefore reads no blob at all. Blobs the database lacks (revisions the
  parser never ingested: branches, commits between tags) are extracted here, in a background job (§2.15)
  spread over `webapp.source_index.workers` (default 2) low-priority `spawn` processes, into one
  cache_engine space (`source-index`, `facts-v<n>`; store `facts`, §2.14, same encoding: `source_facts.encode()`),
  capped at `webapp.source_index.max_mb` (default 1024, least recently used blobs dropped). v3.0 from scratch:
  30,055 `.c`/`.h` files, ~55 s in one process.
- **Revision** (`revision_state(sha)`: `{state: "done", index}` or the job's state): `git ls-tree` of the
  commit, then the facts assembled in two streamed passes (definitions, then calls and tables) into compressed
  sparse rows (callees and callers, each edge with its call site path and line), the member calls, and the ops
  tables with their entries resolved to functions. Nodes are functions and macros by name; a static function
  or a macro defined in a `.c` file is its own node per file and the calls made in that file bind to it, every
  other definition of a name (global functions, header inlines and macros, per-architecture variants) shares
  one node; callees without a C definition (assembly) are nodes without definitions. v3.0: 401k nodes, 1.94M
  calls, 26k member calls, 42k tables with 79k function entries; ~140 MB in memory, assembled in ~8 s from the
  facts.
- **Saved revisions**: an assembled revision is written to the disk cache
  (`BinaryDiskCache("source-index-rev")`, §2.14: one zlib file per commit SHA holding a JSON header, the names
  and paths, and the int32 arrays, `RevisionIndex.to_bytes()` / `from_bytes()`; `FORMAT` and `FACTS_FORMAT`
  are in the key), at most `webapp.source_index.revisions` (default 8) of them, and read back in about a
  second by later requests and after a restart, so a revision is assembled once. The two most recently used
  revisions stay in memory. `status()` reports the database's blob count, the local store and the saved
  revisions.
- **Edges by ARCH**: callers and callees take a per-path filter (`allowed`, cached per ARCH): the call path
  finder drops calls made in other architectures' trees, in the other word size's files of the ARCH's own
  tree, and in user-space trees (`tools/`, `scripts/`, `samples/`, `Documentation/`, `usr/`).
- **Indirect edges** (optional): a call of `->field(` reaches the functions the ops tables assign to `.field`
  (matched by the field name's last component, for any struct: approximate), labelled `via:
  "<struct>.<field>"`, at most 300 per field and node.

### 2.20. Linux man-pages (`webapp/backend/services/man_service.py`, `webapp/backend/routers/man.py`)
The man-pages repository (the entry `is_manpages_entry()` recognises, §2.10) is read from Git at any revision
with the pure parser `parser/man_ast/` (`man_paths`, `man_parser`, `man_facts`; `parser/man_ast/MAN_API.md`).
Man endpoints (§4.13) answer from the request's repository when it is the man-pages, else from the first
available configured man-pages repository; `/api/man/resolve` answers for a kernel revision of the request's
repository.
- **Page files**: `page_map(commit)` lists the tree's page files (`man_paths.page_of_path()`: `man/manS/name.S`
  or `manS/name.S`) once per `(name, section)`, preferring the `man/` path. Root `manS -> man/manS` symlinks of
  the new layout are blobs in the tree listing, so their targets are never listed twice; a request for an
  old-layout path (`man2/read.2`) at a new-layout tag answers with its `man/` path. A name lookup tries the
  given section, then its siblings sharing the base number (`2` -> `2type`, `2const`; `3type` -> `3`), and
  without a section every section in `SECTION_ORDER`; names match exactly, then case-insensitively.
- **Aliases**: a `.so` page (`man_parser.so_target()`) is followed through `man_paths.resolve_so()` (targets are
  relative to the man root) for at most `MAX_SO_HOPS` (5) hops; a loop stops at the last page reached.
- **Index facts**: summaries and alias targets come from the parser's `m_blob_facts` family 6 rows
  (`source_index.db_facts()` / `db_has()`, `"source": "db"`) when every page blob has one, else the missing
  ones are read with one `git cat-file --batch` and extracted with `man_facts.extract()` (`"source": "git"`,
  about 2 s for the 3,150 pages of a recent tag). An alias without a summary shows its target's.
- **Release dates**: `tag_dates()` maps every commit-pointing tag of a repository to the committer date of the
  commit it names (`%(*committerdate)` of an annotated tag, `%(committerdate)` of a lightweight one) and that
  peeled commit; the tag's own creation date is never used, so retroactive tags (`man-pages-1.70`, tagged in
  2014 on a 2004 commit) date from their release commit. Any other revision dates from its commit's committer
  date. Every date below (tag lists, tag choice, kernel release dates, release headers) is this date.
- **Kernel for a man page**: `linux.version` is the `kernel` parameter when it resolves in the kernel repository
  (`kernel_repo` when it names a configured repository that is not the man-pages, else the entry of project
  `linux`, else the first other available one), otherwise the newest final kernel release tag (`vX.Y`, no
  release candidates, stable updates or `next` tags) whose commit is dated on or before the man-pages
  revision's commit, the oldest one when all are later. `linux.syscall` is the page name for section `2`; `linux.symbols` the SYNOPSIS functions and
  identifiers (`fn`, `id` of the facts) that are C identifiers and not keywords, at most 64.
- **Release headers**: in the Git tree, recent pages carry the unreleased placeholders `.TH ... (date)
  "Linux man-pages (unreleased)"`; for a `man-pages-X.Y` revision the page answer substitutes the tagged commit's
  committer date (UTC, `YYYY-MM-DD`) and `Linux man-pages X.Y` on a copy of the document (the cached parse is untouched).
- **Man-pages tag for a kernel**: the newest `man-pages-*` release tag (release candidates left out) whose commit
  is dated on or before the kernel revision's commit, the oldest tag when all are later; when the page is missing there, older
  tags are tried first, then newer ones. One `git cat-file --batch-check` answers every candidate path
  (`man/manS/name.S`, `manS/name.S` for each section to try) at every tag. Without a usable man-pages
  repository, kernel revision or page, the answer is the man7.org URL.
- **Caches** (§2.10): `_TAG_DATES` (per repository), `_PAGE_MAPS` (64 commits), `_INDEXES` (32 commits),
  `_FACTS` (16,384 blobs), `_DOCS` (256 parsed blobs) and `_RESOLVED` (1,024 `(man-pages repository, name,
  section, kernel commit)` answers, scoped by the kernel repository) are `RepoScopedCache`s; tag dates and
  resolve answers are dropped when the refs change (`register_refs_changed`), the commit- and blob-keyed
  entries are immutable.
- **Input validation**: revisions go through `safe_rev()` (`kernel` of a page silently falls back when it does
  not resolve); names match `^[A-Za-z0-9_.:+-]{1,128}$`, sections `^[0-9][a-z]{0,12}$`, paths must pass
  `is_safe_rel_path()` and be page paths; blobs are read by their tree SHA and `cat-file` specs pass
  `is_safe_git_spec()`. Git runs as an argument list, never through a shell.

## 3. Database Schema & Underlying Tables

| Domain Area | Key Database Tables | Primary Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Versions / Git Refs** | `m_git_ref`, `m_commit` | Version and reference identifiers (`ref_id`, `commit_id`, `ref_name`), chronological author dates, commit SHAs |
| **Filesystem & Blobs** | `m_file_blob`, `m_file_name`, `m_bridge_checkpoint`, `m_file_reference` | File instances, content blobs, paths, file types (0=Dir, 1=C, 2=Kconfig, 3=Rust, 4=Asm, 5=Maintainers, 6=Credits, 7=Raw), and compiler-verified `#include` / Kbuild provenance |
